text: Name a property a matrix can have
note: Properties and structured classes. Upper/lower variants are aliases. Role-derived matrices (Hessian, Jacobian, covariance, Laplacian) are excluded

answers.q: Fewer independent eigenvectors than eigenvalues, so no diagonalization. Jordan blocks live here; a random nudge almost surely cures it.
A = Aᵀ. Hessians, covariance and kernel matrices are all symmetric, so their eigenvalues are real.
QᵀQ = I: it preserves lengths and angles. Orthogonal initialization keeps signals from exploding or vanishing in deep nets.
Has an inverse: nonzero determinant, full rank, no zero eigenvalue. Ridge regression adds λI to make XᵀX safely invertible.
Nonzero only on the main diagonal, so multiplying is elementwise scaling. Adam's preconditioner is a diagonal matrix.
xᵀAx > 0 for every x ≠ 0, i.e. all eigenvalues positive. Convex quadratics, Cholesky and valid Gaussian covariances rely on it.
Mostly zeros. Storing only the nonzeros (CSR, COO) is what lets graph and text data fit in memory.
Rank far below its dimensions, so it factors into thin matrices. LoRA fine-tunes an LLM by training only a low-rank update.
Constant along every diagonal. Multiplying by one is a convolution, which is why a conv layer is a (doubly-blocked) Toeplitz matrix.
A = Aᴴ, the complex cousin of symmetric. Real eigenvalues and orthogonal eigenvectors; quantum observables are Hermitian.
Determinant zero: some nonzero vector is mapped to 0, so there is no inverse. Perfectly collinear features make XᵀX singular.
UᴴU = I, the complex version of orthogonal. Quantum gates are unitary, and unitary RNNs use them to keep hidden-state norms constant.
xᵀAx ≥ 0 for every x: all eigenvalues ≥ 0. Every covariance matrix, Gram matrix and valid kernel matrix is PSD.
xᵀAx < 0 for every x ≠ 0. A Hessian like this at a critical point means a strict local maximum.
Has both positive and negative eigenvalues: a Hessian like this marks a saddle point.
All zeros above (or below) the diagonal. Solving Tx = b is just substitution; LU and Cholesky both end in triangles.
Ones on the diagonal, zeros elsewhere; it leaves every vector alone. A residual block x + f(x) is the identity plus a perturbation.
Every entry is 0. Initializing all weights to zero leaves hidden units identical, so symmetry is never broken.

aka: same number of rows and columns
answers.q: As many rows as columns. Only square matrices have determinants, eigenvalues and an ordinary inverse.
Different numbers of rows and columns. Most data matrices are tall: many samples, few features.
Rank equals min(m, n): no column (or row) is redundant. A tall X needs full column rank for XᵀX to be invertible.
Rank below min(m, n), so some columns are combinations of others. Collinear features give a design matrix like this.
Nearly every entry is nonzero, so all n² numbers must be stored. The opposite of sparse.
AAᴴ = AᴴA. Exactly the matrices with an orthonormal eigenbasis, so symmetric, orthogonal and unitary ones are all normal.
A² = A: applying it twice changes nothing. Its eigenvalues can only be 0 or 1.
Aᵏ = 0 for some k. All eigenvalues are zero; strictly triangular matrices are the standard example.
P² = P (and Pᵀ = P if orthogonal). Least squares projects y onto the column space of X using X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ.
Exactly one 1 in each row and column. Multiplying by one reorders rows; they are the corners of the doubly stochastic polytope.
Nonnegative entries and rows (or columns) summing to 1. A Markov chain's transitions; softmax attention weights are row-stochastic.
Aᵀ = −A, so the diagonal is zero. The exponential of a skew-symmetric matrix is a rotation, a common way to parametrize orthogonal layers.
A = PDP⁻¹: a full set of eigenvectors. Almost every matrix is; the defective ones are the exception.
Condition number near 1: small input errors stay small. Orthogonal matrices are perfectly conditioned, κ = 1.
Huge condition number: tiny input changes blow up the solution. The normal equations square the condition number, so avoid them.
Square blocks along the diagonal, zeros elsewhere: independent subproblems. Grouped convolutions are block-diagonal weight matrices.
Nonzeros only within a few diagonals of the main one. Solving costs O(n·b²) for bandwidth b instead of O(n³).
Nonzeros only on the main diagonal and its two neighbors. Solved in O(n) by the Thomas algorithm; Lanczos produces them.
Aᴴ = −A: the complex version of skew-symmetric. Eigenvalues are purely imaginary, and its exponential is unitary.
xᵀAx ≤ 0 for every x. The Hessian of a concave function is negative semidefinite everywhere.
Just uvᵀ: a column times a row. Hebbian updates, LoRA with r = 1 and the Sherman–Morrison formula are all about rank-one terms.
A² = I, so it is its own inverse. Reflections and the exchange matrix are involutory.
Each row is the previous one shifted cyclically. The FFT diagonalizes it, so multiplying by one is a circular convolution.
Constant along anti-diagonals, a Toeplitz matrix flipped. Used in time-series embedding, system identification and moment problems.
Rows are powers 1, x, x², …: polynomial fitting as a matrix. Notoriously ill-conditioned as the degree grows.
Entries ±1 with mutually orthogonal rows. Hadamard conjectured one exists for every order 4k; that is still open.
All pairwise inner products of a set of vectors. Always PSD; a kernel matrix is the Gram matrix of the feature vectors.
Entries 1/(i+j−1). Positive definite yet so ill-conditioned that κ is about 10¹³ at size 10; the classic numerical torture test.
Rows and columns both sum to 1. Sinkhorn iteration produces one; Birkhoff says they are mixtures of permutation matrices.
Every entry ≥ 0. Perron–Frobenius gives them a dominant nonnegative eigenvector, which is what PageRank computes.
Every entry > 0 (not to be confused with positive definite). Perron's theorem: a simple, positive dominant eigenvalue.
Its graph is strongly connected: no reordering makes it block triangular. An irreducible Markov chain can reach any state from any other.
Each diagonal entry outweighs the rest of its row. Guarantees invertibility (Gershgorin) and convergence of Jacobi iterations.
Triangular with zeros on the diagonal too. Always nilpotent.

aka: triangular with ones on the diagonal
answers.q: Triangular with 1s on the diagonal, so determinant 1. The L in Doolittle's LU; coupling flows use such Jacobians.
Built from a polynomial's coefficients; its eigenvalues are the roots. NumPy's roots() just computes them.
λ on the diagonal, 1s just above it. The building block of the Jordan form, and the source of defectiveness.
I − 2vvᵀ/vᵀv mirrors space across a hyperplane. Householder QR zeroes a column with one reflection.
Rotates in a single coordinate plane. A sequence of them zeroes entries one at a time in QR.
Orthogonal with determinant +1: turns space without flipping it. The group SO(n).
Nonzeros only on the diagonal and one adjacent diagonal. Golub–Kahan reduces any matrix to it on the way to the SVD.
Triangular plus one extra subdiagonal. Arnoldi produces it, and the QR eigenvalue algorithm starts by reducing to it.
QᵀQ = I for a tall Q (the U in a thin SVD or QR). Preserves norms though it need not be square.
A diagonal matrix with the same entry everywhere, cI. Commutes with every other matrix.
All eigenvalues have negative real part, so ẋ = Ax decays to zero. The stability condition in continuous-time control.
Entries only 0 or 1. Adjacency matrices of unweighted graphs and attention masks are binary.
All entries are integers. Closed under products; unimodular integer matrices have integer inverses.
Zero rows at the bottom, pivots stepping right as you go down. What Gaussian elimination produces.
Describable by far fewer than n² numbers (Toeplitz, circulant, low-rank, ...). Efficient layers like Monarch exploit this.
Zeros come in whole blocks, which GPUs can skip efficiently. Block-sparse attention is the standard way to cut transformer cost.
Entries are roots of unity. Unitary after scaling; its eigenvectors for circulants are exactly its columns, and the FFT factors it.
The identity with one row operation applied. Gaussian elimination is multiplying by a sequence of them.
Diagonal sums to zero, i.e. eigenvalues sum to zero. The Lie algebra sl(n) consists of exactly these.
Nonnegative with some power entrywise positive. A primitive stochastic matrix gives a chain converging to a unique stationary distribution.
Some permutation similarity makes it block upper triangular; its graph is not strongly connected.
Triangular on the level of blocks. Its determinant is the product of the diagonal blocks' determinants.
Aᵏ → 0 as k grows, equivalently spectral radius below 1. Needed for Neumann series and stable linear recurrences.
Aᵏ⁺¹ = A for some k. Idempotent matrices are the period-1 case.
A − I is nilpotent, so every eigenvalue is 1. Unitriangular matrices are unipotent.
Off-diagonal entries ≥ 0. Then exp(tA) stays entrywise nonnegative: the generator of positive systems like compartment models.
A Z-matrix whose eigenvalues all have positive real part. Discretized elliptic PDEs give them.
All off-diagonal entries ≤ 0. The M-matrices are the Z-matrices with the right spectrum.
All principal minors are positive. Makes the linear complementarity problem uniquely solvable.
A symmetric positive definite Z-matrix. Finite-difference Laplacians are the standard example.
xᵀAx ≥ 0 only required for x ≥ 0. Weaker than PSD, and checking it is co-NP-hard.
A = BBᵀ with B entrywise nonnegative. Strictly stronger than being PSD and nonnegative.
Both PSD and entrywise nonnegative. A tractable relaxation of completely positive.
Every minor (determinant of a square submatrix) is positive. Vandermonde matrices with increasing positive nodes are.
Every minor is ≥ 0. Closed under products; Pascal matrices are the textbook example.
Every square submatrix has determinant 0 or ±1. If the constraint matrix is TU, LP vertices are integral. Network matrices are TU.
Integer entries and determinant ±1, so the inverse is also integral. The change-of-basis matrices of lattices.
det A = 1: orientation- and volume-preserving. Flows built from unitriangular layers have it.
Entries 1/(xᵢ − yⱼ). Has an explicit determinant formula; Hilbert matrices are special cases.
Binomial coefficients in matrix form, Pascal's triangle packed into a matrix. Symmetric positive definite with determinant 1.
Entries min(i,j)/max(i,j). Symmetric positive definite and a standard test matrix, with a known tridiagonal inverse.
Unchanged by a 180° rotation: aᵢⱼ = aₙ₊₁₋ᵢ,ₙ₊₁₋ⱼ. Symmetric Toeplitz matrices are centrosymmetric.
Symmetric about the anti-diagonal. Every Toeplitz matrix is persymmetric.
Symmetric about both main diagonals, i.e. symmetric and persymmetric.
Nonzero only on the diagonal from bottom-left to top-right. The exchange matrix J reverses the order of a vector.
Zero main diagonal. Distance matrices and simple-graph adjacency matrices are hollow.
Every entry is 1: the rank-one matrix 11ᵀ, with eigenvalue n.
MᵀJM = J. Preserves the symplectic form of Hamiltonian mechanics, which is why symplectic integrators conserve energy so well.
JA is symmetric, so eigenvalues come in ±λ pairs. The matrix behind algebraic Riccati equations (LQR).
Ones on one off-diagonal, shifting the entries of a vector by one place. Nilpotent, unless made cyclic.
Identity plus one off-diagonal entry. Slides space along an axis, keeping volume (det 1).
A permutation matrix whose ones may be −1. The symmetries of the hypercube.
One nonzero per row and column: a permutation times a diagonal.
Minimal polynomial has lower degree than the characteristic polynomial. A repeated eigenvalue with several Jordan blocks does it.
Minimal polynomial equals the characteristic polynomial; similar to a companion matrix.
A = Aᵀ with complex entries: not Hermitian. Takagi factorization is its special case of the SVD.
Nonnegative with row sums at most 1: a Markov chain that can leak probability, e.g. absorbing states.
Symmetric with a positive definite top-left and negative definite bottom-right block. KKT systems in interior-point methods look like this.
Nonzeros on the main diagonal and two on each side. Fourth-order finite differences produce them.
Nonzero only on the diagonal plus the first row and column, like an arrow pointing at the top-left.
Toeplitz structure at the level of blocks. A 2-D convolution is a BTTB matrix.
Circulant at the level of blocks. A periodic 2-D convolution is a block-circulant matrix with circulant blocks, diagonalized by the 2-D FFT.
Sum of a Toeplitz and a Hankel matrix. Arises with trigonometric transforms like the DCT and DST.
Like circulant but wrapped entries flip sign. Diagonalized by a twisted DFT; central to polynomial arithmetic mod xⁿ + 1.
Kailath's measure of how far a matrix is from Toeplitz: a small displacement rank allows fast O(n log² n) algorithms.
Low displacement rank with respect to diagonal operators. Toeplitz and Vandermonde matrices can be converted into this form.
Every submatrix on or above the diagonal has rank ≤ 1, so it is stored in O(n) and its inverse is tridiagonal.
Off-diagonal blocks have low rank. A generalization of semiseparable and tridiagonal.
Hierarchically semiseparable: a tree of low-rank off-diagonal blocks with nested bases, allowing near-linear-time solves.
Off-diagonal blocks are low-rank at every scale of a recursive partition. Compresses kernel and PDE operators to near-linear cost.
Hierarchically off-diagonal low-rank: low-rank blocks off the diagonal at every level of a binary partition.
aᵢⱼ + aₖₗ ≤ aᵢₗ + aₖⱼ for i<k, j<l. The SMAWK algorithm finds row minima in linear time; sorted 1-D transport costs are Monge.
A product of log n sparse factors, each pairing entries stride apart: the FFT's structure, learned as a parametrized layer by Dao et al.
Dao et al. 2022: permutations interleaved with two block-diagonal factors. A hardware-friendly structured replacement for dense layers.
